data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference inevitably smuggles induction back in; Popper's attempt to separate 'corroboration' from 'probability' is semantically unstable when applied to action, as any reason to prefer X over Y for future conduct logically entails an inductive belief that X is more reliable than Y.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can define a form of rationality that does not depend on expectations of future regularity, the charge of smuggling induction fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' is restricted solely to the context of designing new experiments (not practical application), the inductive leap might be avoided.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Action is inherently future-oriented. To prefer Theory A over Theory B for the purpose of building a bridge or administering medicine is to assert that A is more likely to yield successful outcomes than B. Since Popper denies that past tests increase the probability of future success, any preference based on those tests relies on the hidden premise that 'the future will resemble the past' (the principle of induction). Without this premise, the choice between a well-tested theory and a wild guess is rationally arbitrary.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
